messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rodrigo is a 67-year-old widowed Latin American man who has worked as a prosecutor for over three decades, a career built on the conviction that the law could impose order on a dangerous world. He came to the clinic after months of resistance, referred by his cardiologist, who had grown concerned that Rodrigo's escalating hypervigilance and sleep disruption were straining his heart. What brought him finally to sit across from a therapist was not the cardiologist's warning, but a morning in the courthouse when he found himself unable to enter a conference room because a child — the young daughter of a witness — was seated inside. He stood in the hallway for eleven minutes, unable to move, and for the first time in his professional life he could not explain his own behavior in terms the law would recognize.

The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Rodrigo had been invited to the home of a colleague, someone he had known for years, a man he had trusted. At some point during the evening, in a room that was warm — the heating turned too high, a specific, close, suffocating heat — he was sexually assaulted by this person. A child belonging to the household was asleep in an adjacent room, and at one point during the assault Rodrigo heard the child stir and call out. That sound, the warmth of the room, and the face of someone he had known — these became the architecture of his trauma, pressed into his nervous system with a precision that no subsequent reasoning has been able to dismantle.

In the weeks that followed, the memories did not recede. They arrived without invitation — vivid, fully formed, and stripped of any temporal distance. Rodrigo described them not as recollections but as re-entries: the heat on his skin, the colleague's face, the child's voice from the other room, all present-tense and immediate. When the memories forced themselves into his mind, they dragged with them a cascade of belief: that his body had been permanently altered, that something essential had been broken inside him, that he was contaminated in a way no amount of showering could address. He had come to understand the world as irredeemably dangerous — not as an abstract philosophical position but as a felt certainty, the way a man understands gravity. These appraisals did not sit passively alongside the memories; they fed back into them, deepening their emotional charge and ensuring that when a memory surfaced, it arrived already weighted with the conviction that what had happened confirmed something true and permanent about his vulnerability.

The appraisals also reshaped his relationship to his own triggers. Because he had come to believe the world was dangerous and his body damaged, the presence of anyone he knew — a colleague, a neighbor, a former friend — became not a source of comfort but a source of threat, a reminder that proximity to known people had not protected him. Children, whose voices and presence were woven into the sensory fabric of that night, became unbearable to be near. A particular warmth on his skin — the close, radiating heat of an overheated room — could send him back entirely. These triggers, in turn, reliably returned him to the memory, which renewed the appraisals, which sharpened the triggers further, a cycle that had been tightening for over a year.

His threat monitoring had become exhaustive. In every room he entered — and this included the courtrooms and offices where he had spent his professional life — he now scanned immediately for exits, catalogued potential weapons, and assessed sightlines. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely, which had narrowed his world considerably; a man who had once traveled for depositions now declined cases requiring out-of-town work. The hypervigilant scanning itself kept the threat system activated, so that the very act of monitoring for danger kept the memories close and accessible, ready to be triggered by the next warm room, the next familiar face, the next child's voice in a hallway.

Rodrigo came to therapy hoping, quietly, that someone could explain to him what had happened to his mind. What he feared most was that nothing could be undone — that the contamination he felt, the damage to his body, the world's irreversible danger, were simply the truth, and that the man he had been before that evening was gone.
